concepts.title: The Plenoptic Function
concepts.one_liner: The plenoptic function is a full description of all light rays traveling across space, defining intensity based on position, direction, wavelength, and time.
concepts.content:
The plenoptic function describes what can potentially be seen by capturing the information about the world contained in the light filling a region of space. Given a scene, it provides a full description of all the light rays that travel across the space. The function tells us the light intensity of a light ray passing through the three-dimensional (3D) point $(X, Y, Z)$ from the direction given by the angles $(\psi, \phi)$, with wavelength $\lambda$, at time $t$: $$L(X, Y, Z, \psi, \phi, \lambda, t)$$ In practice, time is often ignored and continuous wavelength is replaced by three color channels. The function can be represented in a parametric form $L_{\theta}$ where the parameters $\theta$ are adapted to represent each specific scene.

(see figure: Plenoptic function @Adelson91. The figure shows a slice of the plenoptic function at four locations. Two of the locations are in free space, and two other locations are inside a pinhole camera.)

An image is formed by summing all the light rays that reach each sensor on a camera, which corresponds to summing over a section of the plenoptic function. Inside a pinhole camera, the plenoptic function has most values set to zero, with non-zero values only at specific directions at each location to form an image of the exterior.
concepts.motivation_md: The plenoptic function provides a unified mathematical framework to describe all available visual information in a scene. It serves as the theoretical foundation for computer vision and graphics, allowing researchers to treat image formation as the process of sampling a subset of this high-dimensional light field.
concepts.recap_md: - The plenoptic function $L(X, Y, Z, \psi, \phi, \lambda, t)$ describes the intensity of every light ray in a volume.

concepts.title: Radiance Field
concepts.one_liner: A radiance field is a function that assigns color and volumetric density to every point in space, often including viewing direction.
concepts.motivation_md: Radiance fields allow for the representation of complex 3D geometry and appearance (like transparency and specularity) in a continuous format that is well-suited for differentiable rendering and neural optimization.
concepts.recap_md: - A radiance field maps spatial coordinates and viewing angles to RGB color and density $\sigma$.

key_passage.text: A radiance field is a representation of part of the plenoptic function, based on the idea that the optical content of a scene can be modeled as a cloud of colorful particles with different levels of transparency. We will presently define a radiance field $L$ as a mapping from the coordinates in a scene to color and density (i.e. transparency) values of the scene content at those coordinates.

motivation.text: Such a representation can be rendered into images using volume rendering, which we will learn about in The angular coordinates $\psi$ and $\phi$ allow that an object's color be different depending on the angle we look at it, which is the case for shiny surfaces and many other materials.

concepts.title: Vector Fields
concepts.one_liner: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector to each position in space.
concepts.content: Vector fields are functions that assign a vector to each position in space. For example, a vector field might be defined as $f: X, Y, Z \rightarrow v_1, v_2$, where $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are spatial coordinates and $v_1$ and $v_2$ are the resulting values. Radiance fields are a specific application of vector fields used to represent scenes.
concepts.motivation_md: Vector fields provide a general mathematical language for describing spatially varying properties, such as fluid flow, electromagnetic forces, or, in this context, the visual properties of a 3D scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Vector fields map spatial coordinates to a vector of values.

key_passage.text: Radiance fields are an example of vector fields, which are functions that assign a vector to each position in space.

concepts.title: Voxel Fields
concepts.one_liner: Voxel fields are discrete 3D grids that represent values like spatial occupancy or color, functioning as 3D versions of pixels.
concepts.content: Voxel fields, $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow \mathbf{v}$, are discrete fields that represent values $\mathbf{v}$ such as spatial occupancy, flux, or color within a volume. They are essentially 3D pixels. Like pixels, they possess the property of being piecewise constant over cubes defined by their resolution.
concepts.motivation_md: Voxels provide a straightforward way to discretize 3D space for storage and computation, making them useful for medical imaging, 3D modeling, and physical simulations.
concepts.recap_md: - Voxels are discrete 3D units that are piecewise constant over their resolution.

concepts.title: Signed Distance Functions (SDFs)
concepts.one_liner: A signed distance function (SDF) represents the distance from any point in space to the closest surface of an object.
concepts.content: Signed distance functions (SDFs), $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow d$, represent the distance to the closest surface from a given point $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$. This is a useful representation for defining and manipulating 3D geometry.
concepts.motivation_md: SDFs are highly efficient for determining surface intersections and performing geometric operations like boolean unions or subtractions in computer graphics.
concepts.recap_md: - An SDF maps a 3D point to its distance from the nearest surface.

key_passage.text: Signed distance functions (SDFs), $f: X,Y,Z \rightarrow d$, represent the distance to the closest surface to point $[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$.

motivation.text: This is a useful representation of geometry.

concepts.title: Implicit Representation of Fields

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Implicit representations define a field using a function and a finite set of parameters rather than explicitly storing values at every coordinate.
concepts.content: An implicit representation of a field does not explicitly store values at all coordinates. Instead, it records a finite set of parameters for a function that can calculate the field's value at any given coordinate.
concepts.motivation_md: Implicit representations allow for infinite resolution and significantly lower memory usage compared to explicit grids (like voxels) by leveraging the predictive power of functions.
concepts.recap_md: - Implicit representations use parameterized functions instead of explicit data grids.

key_passage.text: Sometimes this is called an implicit representation of the field, since we don't explicitly store the values of the field at all coordinates. Instead we just record a finite set of parameters of a function that can tell us the value of the field at any coordinate.

concepts.title: Parameterized Radiance Fields

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Parameterized radiance fields use differentiable function approximators to represent the mapping from coordinates to color and density.
concepts.content:
There are many different parameterized functions $L_{\theta}$ that can represent a target radiance field $L$. Examples include neural networks or mixtures of Gaussians. The essential property of these functions is that $L_{\theta}$ is differentiable with respect to its parameters $\theta$. This differentiability allows the use of gradient-based optimization to find parameters that best fit the field to a set of images. Regardless of the specific function family used, the module takes coordinates as input and produces colors and densities as output.

(see figure: Module for a parameterized radiance field. We use $\mathbf{R}$ to denote the vector of coordinates $L_\theta$ takes as input.)

Because these are differentiable functions, they can be treated as modules within a larger differentiable computation graph, optimized via backpropagation.
concepts.motivation_md: By parameterizing radiance fields with differentiable functions, we can use standard machine learning optimization techniques to reconstruct 3D scenes from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md: - Parameterized radiance fields must be differentiable to allow for gradient-based optimization.

key_passage.text: There are many different parameterized functions $L_{\theta}$ that could represent our target radiance field $L$. We could use a neural net (e.g., mildenhall2020nerf), or a mixture of Gaussians (e.g., kerbl20233d), or any number of other function approximators. The important property we seek is that the field $L_{\theta}$ is a differentiable function of the parameters $\theta$, hence we can use gradient-based optimization to find a setting of the parameters that yields a desirable field.

motivation.text: we can use gradient-based optimization to find a setting of the parameters that yields a desirable field (we will use this property when we fit a radiance field to images). Later we will put together multiple such modules and use backpropagation to optimize the whole system to fit the field to a set of images.

concepts.title: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs)

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) use neural networks, typically multilayer perceptrons, to model the radiance field of a scene.
concepts.content:
Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model a radiance field $L$ using a neural network $L_{\theta}$. While the original NeRF architecture uses a multilayer perceptron (MLP), other architectures are possible. In the MLP formulation, evaluating the color and density at a single coordinate involves a single forward pass through the network.

To create an explicit representation of the field's values on a grid, the field can be queried at multiple coordinate locations. In this context, a NeRF behaves like a convolutional neural network (CNN) with 1x1 filters, as the MLP is applied to each position in the input grid.

(see figure: NeRF architecture for computing the values at each position in an entire radiance field, sampled on a grid. The $\texttt{pos\_enc}$ refers to positional encoding. You can consider this architecture...)

As established in the original NeRF work, the output layer typically uses a $\texttt{relu}$ activation to ensure density $\sigma$ is non-negative, and a $\texttt{sigmoid}$ activation to ensure $r,g,b$ values fall within the $[0,1]$ range.
concepts.motivation_md: NeRFs provide a powerful way to synthesize novel views of complex scenes by encoding the entire scene's geometry and appearance into the weights of a neural network.
concepts.recap_md: - NeRFs use MLPs to map coordinates to color and density.

concepts.title: Optimization via Volume Rendering

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: Volume rendering enables gradient-based optimization by ensuring that small changes to scene content yield small, non-zero changes to the loss function.
concepts.content: After approximately 2,500 steps of gradient descent, the optimization arrives at a fairly accurate representation of the scene. At this point, object densities are high enough that volume rendering essentially amounts to ray casting, which finds the color of the first surface hit. The primary reason for using volume rendering, even in scenes without volumetric effects, is to facilitate optimization. Volume rendering provides the property that small changes to scene content yield small changes to the loss, resulting in small but non-zero gradients. In contrast, ray casting is an all-or-none operation where small changes to scene content, such as an occluder suddenly revealing an object, can yield drastic changes to rendered images. This makes gradient-based optimization difficult with ray casting but achievable with volume rendering. This benefit is the second major advantage of volume rendering, alongside the ability to model translucency and subsurface effects.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard ray casting creates discontinuous jumps in pixel values when objects move or appear, making gradient-based optimization nearly impossible. Volume rendering smooths these transitions, providing the non-zero gradients necessary for neural networks to learn 3D geometry from 2D images.
concepts.recap_md: - Volume rendering provides a continuous loss function where small scene changes result in small gradient updates.

Ray casting, in contrast, is an all or none operation, and therefore small changes to scene content can yield drastic changes to the rendered images.

concepts.title: The Rendering Equation

position.section_title: Beyond Radiance Fields: The Rendering Equation

concepts.one_liner: The rendering equation is a general formalism for image rendering that models light scattering off surfaces to handle multi-bounce effects.
concepts.content:
The rendering equation, introduced by Kajiya in 1986, provides a formalism for image rendering by directly modeling light scattering off the surfaces in a scene. The equation is written as:

$$L(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') = g(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') \left[ e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}') + \int_S \rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}) L(\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}) d\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime} \right]$$

In this equation, $L(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$ represents the intensity of the light ray passing from point $\mathbf{x}'$ to point $\mathbf{x}$. The function $e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}')$ denotes the light emitted from $\mathbf{x}'$ to $\mathbf{x}$, representing light sources. The function $\rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}',\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime})$ is the intensity of light scattered from $\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}$ to $\mathbf{x}$ by a surface patch at location $x'$, which is related to the bidirectional reflectance distribution function. The variables $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}'$, and $\mathbf{x}^{\prime\prime}$ represent world coordinate vectors. The term $g(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}')$ is a visibility function encoding scene geometry and occlusions; it is 0 if points are not visible to each other, and $1/\lVert \mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}' \rVert ^2$ otherwise to model energy propagation. Essentially, the transport intensity of light between two surface points is the sum of emitted light and the total light intensity scattered toward the destination from all other surface points.
concepts.motivation_md: To accurately simulate how light behaves in a complex environment, researchers needed a mathematical framework that accounts for light sources, surface reflections, and the way light bounces between multiple objects.
concepts.recap_md: - The equation models light intensity as the sum of emitted light and light scattered from all other points in the scene.

key_passage.text: L(x,x') = g(x,x') [ e(x,x') + ∫_S ρ(x,x',x'') L(x',x'') dx'' ] where L(x,x') is the intensity of light ray that passes from point x' to point x, the function e(x,x') is the light emitted from x' to x, and the function ρ(x,x',x'') is the intensity of light scattered from x'' to x by a patch of surface at location x'.

motivation.text: The goal was to introduce a new formalism for image rendering by directly modeling the light scattering off the surfaces composing a scene.

concepts.title: Positional Encoding in NeRFs

position.section_title: Representing Radiance Fields With Parameterized Functions

concepts.one_liner: NeRF uses a positional encoding layer to transform raw coordinates into a Fourier representation, enabling the network to model high-frequency variations in radiance fields.
concepts.content:
NeRF includes a positional encoding layer to transform raw coordinates into a Fourier representation. This uses the same positional encoding scheme as is used in transformers. (see figure: The first layer of NeRF applies positional encoding to the input coordinate values. Here we show the resulting positional codes for all possible input coordinate values $(X,Y)$ within some range.)

Fourier positional encodings are very effective for NeRFs because they help the network to model high frequency variations, which are abundant in radiance fields. In regular Cartesian coordinates, the location $(0,0)$ is much closer to $(1,1)$ than it is to $(100,100)$, but this isn't necessarily the case with Fourier positional codes. Because of this, with Cartesian coordinates as inputs, an MLP will be biased to assign similar values to $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and different values to $(0,0)$ and $(100,100)$. Conversely, with Fourier positional codes as input, this bias is reduced. This makes it so the MLP has an easier time fitting high frequency functions that change in value rapidly, such as assigning very different output values to the locations $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard MLPs struggle to learn high-frequency details when using raw Cartesian coordinates because they are biased toward low-frequency functions. By mapping coordinates to a higher-dimensional Fourier space, positional encoding allows the network to represent sharp edges and fine textures more effectively.
concepts.recap_md: - Maps low-dimensional coordinates to a higher-dimensional Fourier representation.

concepts.title: Volume Rendering
concepts.one_liner: Volume rendering computes pixel colors by integrating radiance and density values along camera rays, modeling the scene as a volume of colored particles.
concepts.content:
Volume rendering is the strategy used for rendering images from radiance fields by taking an integral of the radiance values along each camera ray. This process can be conceptualized as looking into a hazy volume of colored dust, where the integral adds up color values along the ray, weighted by the density of the dust.

The volume rendering equation is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \ell(r) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f}\alpha(t) \, \overbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}^{\text{density}} \, \overbrace{L^c(r(t),\mathbf{D})}^{\text{color}} \, dt\\
    \alpha(t) = \exp \Big(-\int_{t_n}^{t} \underbrace{L^\sigma(r(t))}_{\text{density}} dt\Big)
\end{aligned}$$
where $r(t)$ gives the coordinates of a point at distance $t$ along the ray, $\mathbf{D}$ is the ray direction, and $t_n$ and $t_f$ are near and far cutoffs. The color is modeled as direction-dependent to capture specularities, while density is direction-independent.

The term $\alpha$ represents the probability that a ray has not hit a particle up to distance $t$. If density is zero, the space is empty; if density is infinite, the object is solid and $\alpha$ immediately goes to zero, terminating the ray. Volume rendering generalizes ray casting by allowing for translucency and media like gases or thin films.
concepts.motivation_md: Volume rendering provides a differentiable way to map a 3D radiance field to 2D images. Unlike traditional surface rendering, it can represent semi-transparent materials and provides smooth gradients that are essential for optimizing radiance fields from photographs.
concepts.recap_md: - Integrates color and density along a ray to determine pixel intensity.

concepts.title: Ray Casting
concepts.one_liner: Ray casting is a basic rendering technique that measures the color of the first surface hit by each ray exiting the camera.
concepts.content: Ray casting is a fundamental rendering model used in many basic renderers, such as the standard rasterization pipeline. It can be viewed as a special case of volume rendering where particle density is infinite at surfaces and zero elsewhere; in this scenario, the rendering process reduces to measuring the color of the first surface hit by each ray exiting the camera.
concepts.motivation_md: Ray casting provides a simple, efficient way to render solid 3D geometry by determining visibility and color at the first point of intersection between a ray and a surface.
concepts.recap_md: - Identifies the first intersection point of a ray with scene geometry.

concepts.title: Quadrature Rule for Volume Rendering
concepts.one_liner: The quadrature rule approximates the continuous volume rendering integral as a discrete sum of samples along a ray.
concepts.content:
To compute the volume rendering integral, we approximate it as a discrete sum using a quadrature rule:

$$\begin{aligned}    \ell(r) &\approx \sum_{i=1}^T \alpha_i \, (1-e^{-L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_i)\delta_i}) \, L^c(\mathbf{R}_i, \mathbf{D})\\
    &\alpha_i = \exp\Big(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} L^\sigma(\mathbf{R}_j)\delta_j\Big)\\
    &\delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i
\end{aligned}$$
where the continuous radiance field is replaced by a discrete vector of samples $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$ at world coordinates along the ray $r$.

(see figure: Volume rendering of our Flatland radiance field.)

As visualized in the figure, rays are sent from the camera origin through pixels to query the scene. Each ray is sampled at specific points (drawn as circles). The size of the circle indicates the $\alpha$ value (transmittance), while the color and transparency indicate the density and color of the radiance field. In scenes with solid objects, density is infinite within the object, causing $\alpha$ to go to zero and occluding subsequent points.
concepts.motivation_md: Since the continuous volume rendering integral cannot be solved analytically for complex radiance fields, a discrete approximation is required for numerical computation and implementation in neural networks.
concepts.recap_md: - Converts the continuous integral into a weighted sum of discrete samples.

concepts.title: Stratified Sampling along Rays
concepts.one_liner: Stratified sampling divides a ray into intervals and samples one point uniformly from each, ensuring continuous coverage during optimization.
concepts.content:
Instead of taking samples at evenly spaced increments, we can improve the approximation by chopping the ray into $T$ evenly spaced intervals and sampling one point uniformly within each interval. This ensures that all continuous coordinates will be sampled with some probability over multiple iterations, allowing every point in the continuous space to be supervised during the fitting of a radiance field.

For a ray with origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$, the sampled coordinates $\{\mathbf{R}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{R}_T\}$ are computed as:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{R}_i &= \mathbf{O} + t_i\mathbf{D}\\
    &t_i \sim \mathcal{U}[i-1,i]*\frac{t_f-t_n}{T}+t_n
\end{aligned}$$

where $\mathcal{U}[a,b]$ is the uniform distribution over the interval $[a,b]$.
concepts.motivation_md: Regular grid sampling can lead to aliasing and miss details between samples. Stratified sampling introduces stochasticity that ensures the entire volume is explored over the course of training, leading to better reconstruction of continuous scenes.
concepts.recap_md: - Divides rays into $T$ bins and samples randomly within each bin.

concepts.title: Volume Rendering Pipeline
concepts.one_liner: The volume rendering pipeline maps pixel coordinates to RGB colors by tracing rays, sampling coordinates, and applying the volume rendering integral.
concepts.content:
To compute an image $\boldsymbol\ell$ from a camera, we must find the color of each pixel $\boldsymbol\ell[n,m,:]$. The pipeline consists of three main steps:

1. **Pixel to Ray**: Find the ray (origin $\mathbf{O}$ and direction $\mathbf{D}$) passing through the pixel using the camera origin $\mathbf{O}_{\texttt{cam}}$ and camera matrix $\mathbf{K}_{\texttt{cam}}$.
(see figure: Module for mapping from pixel coordinates to the world coordinates of a ray through that pixel.)

2. **Ray to Coordinates**: Sample world coordinates along the ray, typically using stratified sampling.
(see figure: Module for sampling coordinates along a ray.)

3. **Volume Rendering**: Use the volume rendering integral (via the quadrature rule) to compute the final pixel color.
(see figure: Module for volume rendering of a single ray.)

This pipeline establishes a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values ($n,m \rightarrow r,g,b$), allowing us to infer a radiance field from a set of photos.
concepts.motivation_md: This structured pipeline breaks down the complex task of image synthesis into modular, differentiable steps, enabling the use of gradient-based optimization to solve the inverse problem of vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Converts pixel indices to 3D rays using camera parameters.

key_passage.text: Next we sample world coordinates along the ray, as described previously. Finally, we use the volume rendering integral (using the quadrature rule approximation given previously) to compute the color of the pixel. This pipeline gives a mapping from pixel coordinates to color values: n,m → r,g,b.

concepts.title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: Fitting a radiance field involves optimizing parameters to minimize the reconstruction error between rendered images and observed photographs.
concepts.content:
The goal of fitting a radiance field is to find a representation $L_{\theta}$ that explains a set of observed images. While rendering (view synthesis) is a graphics problem, inferring the radiance field from images is the inverse problem of vision. 

The procedure takes a set of images and their corresponding camera parameters $\{\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}, \mathbf{K}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}, \mathbf{O}^{(i)}_{\texttt{cam}}\}_{i=1}^N$ and produces a parameterized radiance field $L_{\theta}$. We optimize the parameters $\theta$ to minimize the reconstruction error between the rendered images and the observed input images.

[FIGURE:ea67f7c877cd7443]

This can be compared to a magic square puzzle, where we find a square (the radiance field) that integrates to observed row and column sums (the images). Radiance fields like NeRF serve as a constrained hypothesis space; while less general than an unconstrained transformer, they are much more sample efficient and require less data to find a good solution.
concepts.motivation_md: By treating 3D reconstruction as an optimization problem over a differentiable rendering pipeline, we can recover high-quality 3D scene representations from 2D images without requiring explicit 3D supervision.
concepts.recap_md: - Minimizes the difference between rendered and real pixel colors.

concepts.title: Computation Graph for Rendering

position.section_title: Fitting a Radiance Field to Explain a Scene

concepts.one_liner: The NeRF computation graph connects camera parameters, ray sampling, and volume rendering into a fully differentiable pipeline for image synthesis.
concepts.content:
Given a radiance field $L_{\theta}$, an image is rendered using the volume rendering process. The entire computation graph is designed to be fully differentiable, which is critical for fitting parameters to data. 

(see figure: Full NeRF pipeline for rendering an image.)

In this graph, camera parameters are input into the $\texttt{pixel2ray}$ module. The resulting direction $\mathbf{D}$ and the sampling points $\mathbf{t}$ computed by $\texttt{ray2coords}$ are then passed to the $\texttt{vrender}$ module to produce the final output.
concepts.motivation_md: A fully differentiable computation graph allows for the use of backpropagation to update the weights of the neural radiance field, enabling the system to learn 3D geometry and appearance directly from 2D image loss.
concepts.recap_md: - Links camera geometry, coordinate sampling, and volumetric integration.

prereq.rationale: Implicit representations are a method for defining fields, such as radiance fields, using functions rather than explicit coordinate grids.
Parameterized radiance fields are a specific implementation of implicit representations using differentiable function approximators.
Positional encoding is a critical layer within the NeRF architecture used to transform raw input coordinates.
Volume rendering is defined as the strategy for rendering images specifically from radiance fields by integrating values along rays.
The quadrature rule is a specific numerical technique used to approximate the continuous volume rendering integral.
Stratified sampling is used to improve the approximation of the volume rendering integral by ensuring continuous coverage of the space.
The second step of the pipeline involves sampling coordinates along the ray, typically using stratified sampling.
The final step of the pipeline applies the quadrature rule to compute the pixel color from the sampled coordinates.
Fitting a radiance field involves optimizing the parameters of a parameterized representation to explain observed images.
The computation graph is specifically designed to be differentiable to facilitate the fitting of radiance field parameters to data.
The computation graph connects input parameters to the final output via the volume rendering process.
This concept explains the specific pedagogical and mathematical advantages of using volume rendering for gradient-based optimization.
The rendering equation's primary variable, L(x, x'), represents the radiance or intensity along a ray, which is the fundamental unit of a radiance field.
The rendering equation provides the physical and mathematical basis for how the plenoptic function is determined by light-surface interactions in a scene.
A radiance field is defined as a specific representation of the plenoptic function, modeling scenes as clouds of particles.

overlay.rationale: Implicit representations calculate values via functions, whereas voxel fields explicitly store values at specific coordinates.
NeRFs are a specific type of parameterized radiance field that uses neural networks as the function approximator.
Ray casting is described as a special case of volume rendering where density is infinite at surfaces and zero elsewhere.
Stratified sampling provides the discrete coordinates used as inputs for the quadrature rule's summation.
Volume rendering provides smooth gradients for optimization, whereas ray casting is an all-or-none operation that makes gradient-based optimization difficult.
While the rendering equation focuses on surface scattering, volume rendering is a related technique for evaluating light transport through participating media.
Vector fields are introduced as a general class of functions, with radiance fields cited as a specific application for scene representation.
Voxel fields are discrete mappings from 3D coordinates to vectors, fitting the general definition of a vector field.
An SDF is a scalar-valued field, which can be viewed as a 1D special case of the more general vector field mapping.
